Different molecular forms of the same element are allotropes (O2, O3). I can't see the lecture wording itself, but this is the standard term.

The C=O double bond can sit on either of the two equivalent O atoms of the COO- group; the CH3 part has no alternative placement.
The real molecule is a resonance hybrid (not flipping between forms); the 3rd bonding pair is delocalized, so each bond order is 1.5 (between 148 and 121 pm).
CO3 2- has 3 equivalent structures (C=O to any one O); CH4, NH3, and H2O have only single bonds and one structure each.
The resonance arrow links contributing structures of one species; it doesn't stand for equilibrium or atom movement.
18 e-: H-C(=O)-O-; the double bond can go to either O, giving 2 structures, so the C-O bond order is (2+1)/2 = 1.5.
When an atom has single and double bonds to atoms of the same element, the double bond can be moved, which gives equivalent resonance forms.
NO3- has 3 equivalent resonance structures; the hybrid has three identical N-O bonds, each with bond order 4/3.
24 e-: HO-C(=O)-O-; C-OH is always single (1). The other two share one double bond over 2 resonance forms (1.5). The lowest bond order is the longest, so C-OH.

Bond energy is the energy that must be absorbed to break 1 mol of the bonds in the gas phase; the same amount is released when they form.

FC = V - lone e- - bonds. C: 4 - 2 - 3 = -1; O: 6 - 2 - 3 = +1. The sum is 0 for neutral CO.
O: 6 - 6 (3 lone pairs) - 1 (one bond) = -1; H is 0, so the sum is the ion's 1- charge.
N: 5 - 0 lone e- - 4 bonds = +1; each H is 0, so the sum matches the 1+ charge.
S=C=S has FC 0 on every atom. S≡C-S has FC +1/-1, so it is worse. Option 2 uses 20 e- (CS2 has 16), so it is invalid.
The formal charges in any valid structure must sum to the species' overall charge, -2 for SO4 2-.
